summary: ARES is an interactive application developed in Python to plan and evaluate science routes for human exploration in Jezero Crater on Mars. It combines orbital images, geological maps, elevation models, and photographs from the Perseverance rover to calculate total distances at pixel scale and evaluate slopes in profiles every 10 meters. The tool addresses this challenge by allowing users to adjust operational variables, such as walking speed, time at each station, and safety margins, and compare two main routes: Route A (which optimizes time and distance) and Route B (which maximizes scientific results by visiting the three key stations studied by the rover). This work is important for the study of Mars because it works with astrobiological research on the past habitability and strategic decision-making, searching a balance between scientific priorities, terrain difficulty and astronaut safety.
details:
Overview & Operational Mechanics

ARES (Interactive Route and EVA Planning Tool in Jezero Crater) is a web-based mission planning simulator designed to evaluate human Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) across a 900700m sector of Jezero Crater’s western delta on Mars (centered at 18.4541N,77.4050E). Calibrated to a unified scale of 1meterperpixel, the application synthesizes orbital imagery, elevation models, regional geology, and ground-level photographs from NASA’s Perseverance rover. Users can dynamically toggle map layers, zoom into terrain features, inspect three astrobiologically significant stations—Enchanted Lake, Skinner Ridge, and Wildcat Ridge—and configure mission constraints, including walking speed, science duration per station, total suit autonomy, and contingency reserves. Starting and ending at Perseverance’s Sol 427 reference point, ARES evaluates two modeled traverses: Route A (436.7m, visiting one station) and Route B (2,204.9m, visiting all three stations along historical rover paths from Sols 428–557). By computing horizontal distance, cumulative positive elevation gain, and slope profiles every 10 meters .The engine filters out paths that exceed the time budget and recommends the optimal route aligned with the user's selected priority: Science, Terrain, or Time.

Key Advantages & Creative Approach

Rather than offering a passive planetary map viewer, ARES transforms Mars cartography into an interactive trade-off laboratory. Its creative core lies in bridging remote orbital sensing with actionable surface science—pairing specific sedimentary formations (such as sulfate-bearing fine sediments at Wildcat Ridge and stratified sandstones at Skinner Ridge) with tailored field protocols, proposed instruments, and research objectives. Operationally, the platform delivers three core benefits:

Dynamic Scenario Simulation: Mission planners and students can test "what-if" constraints in real time—for example, observing how reducing suit autonomy from four hours to two hours immediately shifts route feasibility from Route B to Route A.

Intuitive Hazard Profiling: Slope angles sampled every 10 meters are translated into a four-tier color-coded difficulty scale—green (<5), yellow (5–10), orange (10–15), and red (15)—exposing steep gradients at a glance.

Zero-Dependency Portability: Easy to use offline: it runs on basic Python, HTML, and CSS, needs no extra programs, and opens locally with python3 atlas.py

Intended Impact

Jezero Crater is one of the most promising places in the solar system to look for signs of ancient life. Billions of years ago, it contained a lake fed by a river, and the sediments in its delta may have preserved traces or evidence of past microorganisms.mars.nasa+2

ARES aims to make the decision-making behind planetary surface missions easier to understand. By letting users take on the role of mission planners, the tool shows that exploring Mars is not only about finding scientifically valuable places. It also involves considering the dangers of the terrain, the limited time available to keep the crew alive, and the need to leave enough room for safety.

In this way, ARES helps people better understand the balance that future human missions will need to find: taking advantage of important scientific opportunities without putting the crew at risk.

Technical architecture and data sources

The system is organized into separate modules. This keeps the calculations and server logic separate from the data and the interface that users see.

Programming languages and tools

The prototype was developed in Python 3. It uses Python’s built-in HTTP server and unit-testing framework. The web interface was built with HTML5 and CSS3.

Code structure

The project is divided into several files:

planificacion.py: calculates movement, slopes, and route recommendations based on several criteria.

atlas.py: runs the local server and displays maps and charts.

plantilla.html: contains the interactive controls for the interface.

datos/terreno.json and datos/estaciones.json: store terrain and scientific-station data.

test_planificacion.py: includes automated tests to check that the calculations work correctly.

Scientific data used

The system uses high-resolution HiRISE orbital images, with a resolution of about 0.25 meters per pixel, and digital terrain models with a resolution of about 1 meter per pixel. It also includes the geological map of Jezero created by Sun and Stack in 2020 and published by the USGS as Scientific Investigations Map 3464 at a scale of 1:75,000. Finally, it uses the coordinates of the route traveled by NASA’s Perseverance rover, along with surface images taken during the mission.

Engineering Factors & Scope Considerations To ensure scientific rigor and transparency, our team incorporated critical operational variables while clearly defining prototype boundaries:

Two-way slope risk : Terrain difficulty is assessed using the absolute value of the slope angle, ∣θ∣, measured every 10 meters. This ensures that a steep downhill section triggers the same warning as an equally steep uphill one. Cumulative elevation gain, however, counts only positive changes in altitude.

Safety margins and tie-breaking criteria: The total time includes travel, scientific work, and extra time for unexpected delays. If more than one route can be completed within the available time, the system chooses the safest one. If two routes are equally safe, it chooses the one that takes less time.

Model limitations : Sampling every 10 meters may miss small obstacles, such as individual rocks. Also, the fact that a rover can traverse a route does not automatically mean that a person could do so safely. Real-time variables—such as radiation, dust storms, and the energy or metabolic demands of the spacesuit—are left for future versions of the system
